lead: On the day after Pentecost the Roman Rite honours the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church. The readings take us to two moments: the garden, where after the first sin God promises enmity between the serpent and the woman and her offspring, and the Cross, where Jesus gives his mother to the beloved disciple and the disciple to his mother. The Lectionary also allows Acts 1:12–14, where the apostles pray “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” before Pentecost.
Psalm 87 sings of Zion, the city of God, as the mother of the peoples: “This one was born there.” The Church, the new Jerusalem, is our mother, and Mary is the mother of the Church.

r.h: I will put enmity between you and the woman
set: The man and the woman have eaten from the tree, their eyes have been opened, and they have hidden themselves from God among the trees of the garden (3:1–8). Now God comes to find them. The Lectionary leaves out vv. 16–19, the consequences for the woman and the man, and adds v. 20, where the man names his wife Eve.

Background. This is part of the second account of creation (2:4b–3:24). It tells in the language of images a real event at the beginning of human history, the first sin, as the Catechism teaches (CCC 390). The serpent is the figure of the tempter, whom the Book of Revelation calls “that ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan” (Revelation 12:9).
str: vv. 9–10: “Where are you?” I was afraid and hid.
vv. 11–13: God questions; the man blames the woman, the woman blames the serpent.
v. 14: the curse on the serpent.
v. 15: enmity between the serpent and the woman, his offspring and hers.
v. 20: Eve, mother of all living.
kw: God’s first question to fallen man. Not because God does not know, but to call the man out of hiding. It is the question of a Father seeking his child.
A lasting hostility. God himself puts it: the human race will not be left in friendship with evil.
It can mean descendants in general or one descendant. Christian tradition reads it of Christ, the offspring of the woman who defeats the serpent.
The name sounds like the Hebrew word for “living”. Eve is “the mother of all living”. The Fathers called Mary the new Eve, mother of all who live in Christ.
vv: But the Lord God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
Sin makes us hide; God comes looking. The whole of salvation history begins with this search.
The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.”
The first fruit of sin is broken relationship: the man blames the woman, and even God who gave her. The unity of the first couple is wounded.
I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike your head, and you will strike his heel.

Even before the punishment of the man and woman, God speaks a promise. The Hebrew says “he” (or “it”), meaning the offspring; the old Latin Vulgate read “she”, and so many paintings show Mary crushing the serpent. The Church’s faith does not rest on that reading: the victory belongs to Christ, and Mary shares in it as his mother, wholly on his side against the serpent.
The man named his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all living.
After the sentence of death, the man gives his wife a name of life. Hope is not lost.
ch: The Catechism calls Genesis 3:15 the “Protoevangelium”, the first announcement of the Messiah and Redeemer, of a battle between the serpent and the Woman, and of the final victory of a descendant of hers. Many Fathers and Doctors of the Church see the Woman as Mary, the mother of Christ, the new Eve (CCC 410–411). St Irenaeus taught that the knot of Eve’s disobedience was loosed by Mary’s obedience; what the virgin Eve bound by unbelief, the Virgin Mary loosed by faith. The Council quotes him (Lumen Gentium 56), and it recalls that the promise of victory over the serpent foreshadows Mary (Lumen Gentium 55). Blessed Pius IX cited this verse in defining the Immaculate Conception in 1854.

r.h: Woman, here is your son. Here is your mother
set: Jesus has been crucified, and the soldiers have divided his clothes (19:23–24). Only John tells that the mother of Jesus stood near the Cross. In John’s Gospel she appears only twice, at Cana (2:1–12) and at Calvary, and she is never named; she is “the mother of Jesus”. At Cana Jesus said to her, “Woman, ... My hour has not yet come” (2:4). Now the hour has come (13:1).
str: v. 25: the women near the Cross.
vv. 26–27: “Woman, here is your son.” “Here is your mother.” The disciple takes her into his own home.
vv. 28–30: “I am thirsty”; the sour wine; “It is finished”; he gives up his spirit.
vv. 31–33: the legs of Jesus are not broken.
v. 34: the soldier pierces his side; blood and water flow.
kw: A respectful form of address, used also at Cana (2:4). It recalls “the woman” of Genesis 3:15 and the mother of the new humanity.
Literally “into his own”: among the things that were his. The disciple welcomes Mary into his life as a treasured gift.
Accomplished, brought to its goal. The work the Father gave the Son is complete (17:4).
Literally “handed over the spirit”. He dies, and his death already looks towards the gift of the Spirit to the Church.
vv: standing near the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
They stand. Mary does not flee. She who said “Here am I, the servant of the Lord” (Luke 1:38) remains faithful at the hour of the Cross.
When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing beside her, he said to his mother, “Woman, here is your son.”
The beloved disciple is not named. The Church sees in him every disciple whom Jesus loves. From the Cross Jesus gives his mother a new motherhood.
Then he said to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” And from that hour the disciple took her into his own home.
This is more than a son providing for his widowed mother. It is the gift of the hour: Mary becomes mother of the disciples, and the disciple receives her.
When Jesus had received the wine, he said, “It is finished.” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
He bows his head first, then hands over his spirit: in John he lays down his life of his own accord (10:18).
Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.

John insists that he saw it (19:35). The Fathers saw in the blood and water the sacraments of the Eucharist and Baptism, and the Church born from the side of Christ, as Eve was formed from the side of Adam.
ch: The Council teaches that “from the side of Christ as he slept the sleep of death upon the Cross there came forth the wondrous sacrament of the whole Church” (Sacrosanctum Concilium 5; CCC 766). Lumen Gentium says that Mary, standing at the Cross, was given by the dying Jesus as mother to his disciple (Lumen Gentium 58; CCC 964), and, quoting St Augustine, that she is truly mother of the members of Christ, because she cooperated by her love so that the faithful might be born in the Church (Lumen Gentium 53; CCC 963). St Paul VI proclaimed Mary Mother of the Church on 21 November 1964, at the Council. Saint John Paul II wrote that the disciple’s taking Mary “into his own” is the model for every Christian who entrusts himself to her (Redemptoris Mater 45).

qa: Why does Jesus call his mother “Woman”?

It is not cold or disrespectful. In Greek it was a courteous form of address. In John it has a deeper meaning: Mary at Cana and at the Cross is “the woman” whose offspring defeats the serpent (Genesis 3:15), the new Eve, the mother of the new people of God. Jesus speaks to her not only as her son, but as Redeemer, giving her a mission.
Does calling Mary “Mother of the Church” put her in the place of Christ?

No. The Council teaches that there is one mediator, Christ, and that Mary’s maternal role does not obscure or diminish his unique mediation but shows its power; it flows from his merits and depends on them entirely (Lumen Gentium 60). Mary is the first and most excellent member of the Church, and at the same time its mother (Lumen Gentium 53). She always leads us to her Son: “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5).
rite: In 2018 Pope Francis inscribed this memorial in the General Roman Calendar for the Monday after Pentecost (decree Ecclesia Mater of the Congregation for Divine Worship, 11 February 2018), so that the Church, born at Pentecost, might honour the Mother who prayed with the apostles for the Spirit. It is an obligatory memorial. With it the Church in the Roman Rite resumes Ordinary Time, in the seventh week this year; the vestments are white for the memorial.
study: God asks Adam, “Where are you?” Where am I hiding from God now?
Mary stood near the Cross. Whose suffering am I called to stand near, without running away?
The disciple took Mary into his own home. What place does Mary have in my home and my family prayer?
